questions.q: What problem does the LET function actually solve?
options: It lets you name an intermediate calculation once inside a formula, instead of repeating the same sub-expression multiple times
It lets you create a new custom Excel function permanently
It converts a formula into a macro
It automatically sorts a range in ascending order
questions.explain: LET assigns a name to a value or expression so it's calculated once and reused, rather than being written and recalculated repeatedly.

questions.q: In =LET(total, SUM(B2:B10), IF(total>1000, total*0.9, total)), how many times is SUM(B2:B10) actually calculated?
options: Once
Three times
Zero times — it's never calculated
Once per row in the range
questions.explain: LET calculates the SUM(B2:B10) expression a single time when it defines the name 'total', then reuses that stored result everywhere 'total' appears afterward.

questions.q: What is the last argument in every LET function call?
options: The actual calculation that uses the defined names
Another name/value pair
An optional error message
A cell reference to display the result in
questions.explain: After all name/value pairs, LET's final argument is always the calculation that puts those names to use.

questions.q: How many name/value pairs does LET support, and what is a name's scope?
options: Up to 126 pairs, and each name only exists inside that one formula
Exactly 1 pair, scoped to the entire workbook
Up to 10 pairs, scoped to the entire worksheet
Unlimited pairs, scoped to all open workbooks
questions.explain: LET supports up to 126 name/value pairs, and unlike a workbook-wide defined name, a LET name is local to that single formula only.

questions.q: Besides readability, what is the other concrete benefit of rewriting a formula with LET?
options: Performance — a repeated sub-expression is calculated once instead of multiple times
It automatically formats the result as currency
It makes the formula compatible with older Excel versions that don't support LET
It removes the need for cell references entirely
questions.explain: Calculating an expensive or volatile expression once instead of several times is a genuine performance win, not just a style choice.
